def: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular repeating 3D pattern, while amorphous solids have particles arranged randomly with no long-range order.
points: Crystalline solids have a definite geometric shape; amorphous solids do not.
Crystalline solids have a sharp, fixed melting point; amorphous solids melt over a range of temperature.
Crystalline solids are anisotropic — properties like refractive index differ with direction. Amorphous solids are isotropic.
Crystalline solids have long-range order; amorphous solids have only short-range order.
When crystalline solids are cut with a sharp tool, they break into pieces with flat faces (cleave). Amorphous solids give an irregular cut.
Examples: NaCl, diamond, quartz are crystalline. Glass, rubber, plastic are amorphous.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Solids"] --> B["Crystalline"]
  A --> C["Amorphous"]
  B --> D["Regular long range order"]
  C --> E["Random short range order"]

example: Quartz (crystalline SiO2) has a sharp melting point and flat faces, while quartz glass (amorphous SiO2) softens gradually over a range of temperature.
tip: Write the comparison as a two-column table in the exam — isotropic/anisotropic and sharp/range melting point are the most asked points.

def: A unit cell is the smallest repeating unit of a crystal lattice; SCC, BCC and FCC describe how particles are packed at the corners, body centre and face centres of a cube.
points: Simple cubic cell (SCC): particles only at 8 corners. Z (atoms per cell) = 8 x 1/8 = 1. Coordination number = 6.
Body-centred cubic (BCC): corners plus one particle at body centre. Z = 8 x 1/8 + 1 = 2. Coordination number = 8.
Face-centred cubic (FCC): corners plus one particle at the centre of each of the 6 faces. Z = 8 x 1/8 + 6 x 1/2 = 4. Coordination number = 12.
Each corner atom is shared by 8 unit cells, so it contributes 1/8 to one cell.
Each face atom is shared by 2 unit cells, so it contributes 1/2 to one cell.
A body-centre atom belongs entirely (1) to that one cell.

diagram.draw: Draw three cubes side by side. First cube: dots only at the 8 corners, label 'SCC, Z=1'. Second cube: dots at corners plus one dot in the middle, label 'BCC, Z=2'. Third cube: dots at corners plus one dot on the centre of each of the 6 faces, label 'FCC, Z=4'.

example: Polonium crystallizes in SCC lattice, so each unit cell contains exactly 1 atom of Po.
tip: Draw all three cells quickly with correct dot positions and write Z and coordination number under each — this is a guaranteed 2-mark diagram question.

def: Packing efficiency is the percentage of the total volume of a unit cell that is actually occupied by the spherical particles.
points: Packing efficiency = (volume occupied by atoms / total volume of unit cell) x 100.
For SCC: atoms touch along the edge, a = 2r, packing efficiency = 52.4%.
For BCC: atoms touch along the body diagonal, a = 4r/sqrt(3), packing efficiency = 68%.
For FCC: atoms touch along the face diagonal, a = 2*sqrt(2)*r, packing efficiency = 74%.
FCC and HCP (close packed structures) have the highest packing efficiency and leave the least empty space (void).
Remaining % of the cell volume is empty space (void volume).
formula: Packing efficiency = (Z x (4/3)pi r^3 / a^3) x 100

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["SCC 52.4%"] --> B["BCC 68%"]
  B --> C["FCC 74%"]
  C --> D["Closest packing least empty space"]

example: For FCC: a = 2*sqrt(2)*r, volume occupied by 4 atoms = 4*(4/3)pi r^3, cube volume = a^3 = 16*sqrt(2)*r^3. Packing efficiency = (16.76/22.6)x100 ≈ 74%.
tip: Memorize the final 3 numbers 52.4%, 68%, 74% along with which structure has which — direct 1-mark questions are common.

def: The density of a crystal can be calculated from the number of atoms per unit cell, molar mass, edge length and Avogadro's number.
points: Density d = (Z x M) / (a^3 x N_A), where Z = atoms per unit cell, M = molar mass, a = edge length, N_A = Avogadro number.
Edge length a must be converted to cm (1 pm = 10^-10 cm) before using in the formula since density is usually in g/cm^3.
a^3 gives the volume of one unit cell in cm^3.
This formula connects the microscopic crystal structure to the bulk density we can measure in the lab.
Rearranging the formula lets us find Z, M or a if the other three quantities are known.
formula: d = Z x M / (a³ x N_A)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Z atoms per cell"] --> D["Density formula"]
  B["Molar mass M"] --> D
  C["Edge length a"] --> D
  D --> E["d = ZM / a cubed NA"]

tip: Always convert pm to cm correctly (1 pm = 10^-10 cm) — unit mistakes are the most common error here.

def: Point defects are irregularities or imperfections at specific points in the otherwise regular arrangement of particles in a crystal.
points: Vacancy defect: a particle is missing from its lattice site; decreases density.
Interstitial defect: extra particles occupy the empty spaces (interstitial sites) between lattice points; increases density.
Frenkel defect: a smaller ion leaves its normal site and occupies an interstitial site, creating a vacancy + interstitial pair; density unchanged (seen in AgCl, AgBr, ZnS).
Schottky defect: equal numbers of cations and vacancies of anions are missing from the lattice to maintain electrical neutrality; decreases density (seen in NaCl, KCl).
Non-stoichiometric defects: metal excess or metal deficiency defects where the ratio of cations to anions differs from the ideal formula, often giving colour or semiconducting behaviour.
Point defects affect electrical conductivity, density and colour of the crystal.
formula: Schottky: equal cation + anion vacancies | Frenkel: ion displaced to interstitial site

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Point Defects"] --> B["Vacancy"]
  A --> C["Interstitial"]
  A --> D["Frenkel pair vacancy and interstitial"]
  A --> E["Schottky cation and anion vacancy"]

example: AgBr shows Frenkel defect because Ag+ is small and can move into interstitial space, while NaCl shows Schottky defect because Na+ and Cl- are similar in size and cannot show Frenkel defect easily.
tip: Pair each defect name with its example compound (AgBr/AgCl for Frenkel, NaCl/KCl for Schottky) — examiners often ask 'give an example' directly.

def: Solids are classified as conductors, semiconductors or insulators based on band theory, and as diamagnetic, paramagnetic or ferromagnetic based on their behaviour in a magnetic field.
points: Band theory: valence band (filled with electrons) and conduction band (empty, higher energy) are separated by an energy gap.
Conductors: valence and conduction bands overlap, so electrons move freely (e.g. metals like Cu, Ag).
Insulators: large energy gap between bands, so electrons cannot jump to the conduction band (e.g. diamond).
Semiconductors: small energy gap, so a few electrons can jump to the conduction band, especially on heating or doping (e.g. Si, Ge).
Diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled by a magnetic field (all electrons paired); paramagnetic substances are weakly attracted (unpaired electrons present).
Ferromagnetic substances are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetized because magnetic domains align in the same direction (e.g. Fe, Co, Ni).
formula: Conductor: no energy gap | Semiconductor: small gap | Insulator: large gap

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Conductor bands overlap"] --> D["Free electron flow"]
  B["Semiconductor small gap"] --> E["Few electrons jump"]
  C["Insulator large gap"] --> F["No electron flow"]

example: Silicon is a semiconductor; doping it with a group 15 element (like P) adds extra electrons, creating an n-type semiconductor with increased conductivity.
tip: Draw the three band diagrams (overlap, small gap, large gap) side by side — this diagram alone can fetch 2 marks.
